node.name: Volunteer with Sunrise Cafe!
node.descriptionText:
Start your morning off on a great note! Join Dwight Hall Monday and Wednesday mornings to volunteer at Sunrise Cafe. Sunrise Cafe is an early morning soup kitchen that serves New Haven's homeless and food-insecure every weekday from 6:30 A.M. to 8:30 A.M. The service site is located at 57 Olive St., just a 15 minute walk from Phelps Gate. Volunteers will meet in front of Phelps Gate at 6:00am, walk together to Sunrise Cafe, and will return to campus by 9:00am.

To sign up, please request to join DWIGHT HALL VOLUNTEER CORPS, and we will approve your request as soon as possible.

Sunrise Cafe has been serving breakfast without charge to New Haven's homeless and hungry since 2015. Each weekday morning, the Cafe welcomes guests to the undercroft of St. Paul and St. James, near Wooster Square and three blocks south of the New Haven Green with white tablecloths, flowers and a rotating menu of fresh, warm, nutritious home-cooked food. Your generosity opens our doors.

Cheerful volunteers take each order individually, deliver the breakfast to our guest and help our paid chefs in the kitchen. Staff and volunteers ensure every guest is warmly welcomed.

Sunrise Cafe is uniquely welcoming and secure, based on trust and mutual respect, and the rapport built between the volunteer servers and our guests. With a warm welcome and just two rules – no drugs on the premises and no arguments – Sunrise has become a community center for the homeless, a place to come every weekday morning and gather with friends.

Hungry friends come for the home-cooked, nourishing breakfast and stay for simple medical services offered by the Cornell Scott Health Center and access to support from social services to find housing.

Sunrise provides a unique opportunity to bridge New Haven's inequalities that separate us from one another. Volunteers come once and become regulars. Guests and volunteers become friends and greet one another on the street.

If you have any questions, email maryann.dang@yale.edu

node.name: Global Nurse Force: Bridging Health and Climate Action
node.descriptionText:
Join the 2026 Global Collaborative Series, a partnership between the University of Michigan School of Nursing, Vanderbilt University School of Nursing, and Yale School of Nursing. This year's theme, Global Nurse Force: Bridging Health and Climate Action, brings together international health leaders to tackle the intersections of global health leadership and climate action through a virtual panel series focused on building climate-resilient healthcare systems and advancing sustainable health equity worldwide.

Featured speaker: Kathleen Groff, DNP, FNP-BC, RN, is a family nurse practitioner with a passion for women's health and a holistic approach to primary care. She has a diverse range of experience in military and college health as well as global women's issues. Some key highlights include advocacy for Afghan women and nation-building, supporting healthy dietary options in impoverished urban communities and caring for survivors of sexual assault and intimate partner violence. 

Dr. Groff was a part of the inaugural team of the Planetary Health Policy Innovation Lab while completing her Doctor of Nursing Practice at Vanderbilt University. With the mentorship of Dr. Carol Ziegler, she explored climate­focused social innovation to address health inequities in our nation. Her work focused on the positive economic, environmental, and health impacts of paid maternity leave policies. 

Dr. Groff is a US Army Veteran who served as the Sexual Assault Medical Director during her time in service. She currently practices at the American University Student Health Center in Washington, D.C.

node.name: Daily Worship at Marquand Chapel
node.descriptionText:
Join us at 11:30am in Marquand Chapel for our daily worship.

Worship in Marquand often draws on a wide variety of inherited Christian traditions, with the worship of many denominations being represented. Beyond that, though, we also pay attention to the rising number of people in Western society who have a lively interest in spirituality but feel no connection to traditional forms of church and worship. So Marquand is also actively engaged in original, creative, and experimental forms of worship, both for committed Christians and for those exploring the faith.

node.name: BIOMES: Understanding urban heat: from space to street, presented by Xuhui Lee, Sara Shallenberger Brown Professor of Climate Science, Yale School of the Environment
node.descriptionText:
Seminar Summary: 
Urban heat is one of the most serious climate threats to society. The problem reflects both concentration of vulnerable populations in cities and the tendency of urban land to create warmer microclimates than natural land. This talk will compare two observational strategies (satellite versus street-level) for quantifying and understanding urban heat. The basic principles of boundary-layer meteorology are used to interpret experimental data on intra-city variations in microclimate and on greenspace mitigation of dry and humid heat. The final part of the talk is a presentation of satellite and street-level observations on slum heat hazards in Global South cities.

node.name: Schwarzman Session - Accessibility as a Core Value from Ideation to Opening Night with DJ Kurs
node.customTimeInstruction: Apply to be part of this conversation
node.descriptionText:
Instructions

This event takes place at the Yale Humanities Quadrangle located at 320 York Street, New Haven, CT. Once entering the building find room number 276 on the second floor. 

Free and open to the public with registration.

Seats are limited, so registrants will automatically be placed on the waitlist and will be notified via email if selected.
If you need technical assistance with registration or require accessible accommodations contact ysc.info@yale.edu.

ASL interpretation provided. No sign language knowledge needed to attend. Come be a part of the conversation!  

Schwarzman Sessions are peer-led gatherings where conversations generate collaborations and move ideas into action. Because seats are limited, registrants will be automatically placed on the waitlist and will be notified via email if they are selected to participate. 

Join DJ Kurs, Artistic Director of Deaf West Theatre, for a lunchtime conversation about building accessibility into creative work from the start. What does access look like at every stage of a project, from the first idea to opening night? How do we make it part of how we work every day, not an afterthought?

One in four Americans lives with a disability. That includes veterans, aging parents, kids, and coworkers, plus the families and friends who buy tickets with them. It’s one of the largest audiences most organizations still miss. Access designed from the beginning is good craft and good business. It makes the work better and opens new markets.

Lunch will be provided! 

ASL interpretation provided. No sign language knowledge needed to attend. Come be a part of the conversation!  

Consider these thought prompts for the discussion:

Spring Awakening at the Tony Awards: YouTube
Behind the scenes of Fidelio with Gustavo Dudamel: YouTube
El Canto de las Manos trailer: YouTube

This event is presented in conjunction with MacMillan Center for International and Area Studies at Yale. This is part of the 2026 Henry E. Howland Memorial Prize awarded to Gustavo Dudamel. See a full schedule of events Nov 16-18 HERE.

node.name: Beyond the Divide: Cynicism, Sincerity, and the Future of American Politics
node.descriptionText:
Since 2018, More in Common has tracked the fault lines of American polarization and discovered that beneath the familiar left-right split, a new divide is emerging: between those who see politics as a war to be won, and those who still believe we can build something together across our differences.

Join Jason Mangone (Executive Director; Jackson ’13) and Nathalie Bussemaker (Senior Research Associate; Yale College ’21) of More in Common to explore how polarization has evolved over the past decade and to tackle the question defining our political moment: Are we destined for a politics of domination — or is there still a path to a shared future, forged through our differences rather than in spite of them?
Presentation will be followed by a conversation facilitated by Yale Democracy Project student leaders.

Sponsored by Cultivating Conversation, the Yale Democracy Project, and Yale Votes.


Please register on Yale Connect or visit: https://cultivatingconversation.yale.edu/events/2026-11-18-beyond-the-divide-cynicism-sincerity-and-the-future-of-american-politics

node.name: YCNCC Visiting Scholar Panel: The Rise of Climate Engineering
node.descriptionText: Can we engineer our way out of climate change? Engineering approaches to averting the worst impacts of climate change, from carbon dioxide removal to solar radiation management, are drawing growing attention. This panel discussion will delve into questions surrounding who decides which planet-cooling technologies get funded, tested and deployed; how we balance geopolitical risks, economic trade-offs and geochemical realities; and the role universities should play in shaping a safe and equitable climate agenda. Panelists David Keith (University of Chicago, YCNCC Fall 2026 Visiting Scholar), Ken Gillingham (Yale School of the Environment), Noah Planavsky (Yale Earth & Planetary Sciences), and Jessica Seddon (Jackson School of Global Affairs) bring perspectives from climate science, economics, and geochemistry. YCNCC Faculty and Associate Professor of Chemical & Environmental Engineering David Kwabi) will moderate.

node.name: Tips & Tricks for Writing Law School Exam Answers
node.descriptionText:
Writing for law school exams is its own genre of writing, one that diverges sharply from how most law school courses dedicate their time. This workshop will offer practical tips for answering issue-spotter questions on law school exams. Examples will be drawn from Torts, Criminal Law, and Evidence, though the tips and tricks are applicable across doctrinal courses (and no prior experience with these courses is necessary).   

Drawing on her experience teaching Evidence at BYU Law School, Graduate Writing Lab Assistant Director Kathryn Blair will present techniques for reading exam questions, strategies for organizing your answers, and approaches to offering a more complete analysis in your responses.  

Intended audience: Yale Law School students.

node.name: ITW: AI in the Classroom (New Date)
node.descriptionText: Generative AI has arrived in our classrooms, but what’s next? How do we have transparent conversations with our students about what these tools are and how or when to use them (or not use them)? In this workshop, we’ll discuss AI policy statements, Yale’s own AI tools and platforms, and how to center equity and accessibility in our conversations about AI for learning. Finally, participants will analyze example AI activities from other instructors and reflect on how and whether they want to integrate AI into their lesson plans or assessments, across a variety of disciplines, and in critical and creative manners. We welcome all levels of expertise with and excitement about AI as we navigate these questions together! Please reach out to Oliver Lucier (oliver.lucier@yale.edu) and Ulas Berk Karli (ulasberk.karli@yale.edu) with any questions
